bp: This tutorial is about systems made of connected parts whose connections and behavior change together. In a social network, a person's opinion can alter who they talk to, and those new conversations can then alter later opinions. In a brain, activity can reshape neural connections, and those changed connections affect future activity. The same pattern appears in disease spread, power grids, and other networked systems: the map of relationships is not just a background drawing, because the map helps decide what happens next. The practical need is prediction and safety under partial knowledge. A planner may want to know whether an outbreak will grow, whether a power system will stay reliable, whether a group will synchronize, or whether a small failure can cascade. The tutorial's subject is how to reason when the network, its strengths, its rules of change, and outside pressures are all partly unknown.
wh: The hard part is that uncertainty enters through several doors at once. One edge may be missing, another may have the wrong strength, a node may react differently than expected, and an outside influence may change over time. In an ordinary static network, a wrong link can already distort the answer. In a dynamical network, the error can feed forward: a slightly wrong contact pattern can change a disease forecast, that forecast can change an intervention, and the intervention can change the later network. The abstract points to fluctuating edge weights, evolving connections, stochastic interactions, unknown contact patterns, changing transmission rates, uncertain demand, and renewable energy variation. These are not small bookkeeping errors. They change stability, synchronization, and cascading failure questions because those outcomes depend on how local changes travel through the whole connected system over time.
naive: A smart beginner might first draw the best available network, choose one set of parameters, run the model once, and treat the answer as the forecast. That is natural because it turns a messy situation into a single map and a single future. It fails because the single map is often only a guess. Unknown contacts in epidemiology, changing neural links, fluctuating edge weights, and variable power demand can all produce different futures from nearly the same starting picture. Another beginner move is to test a few hand-picked alternatives, but that still misses which uncertainties matter most and how combinations of small errors can amplify each other.
ap: The core idea is to make the unknown parts of the dynamical network visible instead of hiding them inside one confident forecast. Uncertainty quantification means naming the pieces that are not known exactly, describing how much they may vary, and tracing how that variation changes the predicted behavior. The tutorial bridges two objects: a network whose nodes and links shape a dynamic process, and a disciplined way to measure uncertainty in model structure, parameters, and outside inputs. Mechanically, this means treating the network not as one fixed diagram but as a family of plausible diagrams and rules. The important question then changes from, What will happen? to, What range of behavior is plausible, which uncertain pieces drive that range, and how reliable is the conclusion about stability, synchronization, or failure spread?
mech: The mechanism starts with a dynamical network description. The inputs are the nodes, the links among them, the strengths or weights of those links, the rules by which activity changes over time, and outside influences such as contact rates, demand, or renewable energy supply. First, the analyst separates what is known from what is uncertain. A link may exist with uncertain strength, a connection may appear or disappear, a transmission rate may vary, or an external load may fluctuate. Second, those uncertainties are represented as ranges, chances, or alternative scenarios, depending on what evidence is available. Third, the dynamic model is run or analyzed across those possibilities so the uncertainty can move through the system rather than remain a note in the margin. Fourth, the outputs are compared: some versions may settle, some may synchronize, some may trigger cascades, and some may make predictions unreliable. Finally, the analyst asks which uncertain inputs changed the outcome most. The result is not just a predicted trajectory. It is a map from uncertain network structure, uncertain parameters, and uncertain outside pressure to a set of possible behaviors and a measure of how much confidence the decision maker should place in each conclusion.
math: The main mathematical objects are a graph, a time rule, and a measured description of uncertainty. The graph is the map: nodes stand for people, neurons, power components, or other units, and links stand for channels through which influence, activity, infection, or load can pass. The time rule says how the state of each node changes as its own condition, its neighbors, and outside forces change. Dynamical systems is the name for studying such rules over time: instead of asking only what the network looks like now, it asks where the whole connected system can move next and whether it settles, oscillates, synchronizes, or breaks. Probability enters because the analyst does not know every link, parameter, or outside shock exactly. It turns incomplete evidence into explicit degrees of belief or ranges of plausible values. Sensitivity analysis is the related idea of asking which uncertain knob matters most: if a small change in one transmission rate greatly changes an outbreak forecast, that knob deserves attention. The tradeoff is detail versus trust. A single forecast is easy to read but can hide fragility; a quantified range is harder to summarize but better matches a world where the map and the process are both uncertain.
dots: This tutorial sits where several recurring conference ideas meet. It is a network paper because the object of study is a set of connected units where neighbors carry influence. It is also a probability paper because the central problem is acting with incomplete, noisy, and changing evidence. It connects to time-series and spatiotemporal work because the answer depends on how signals evolve, not just on a one-time snapshot. It also touches reliability and anomaly concerns: cascading failures in power systems and uncertain outbreaks are cases where wrong confidence can be costly. Compared with graph learning papers that spread evidence through a fixed relationship map, this topic asks what happens when the map itself, the strengths on the links, and the external pressures are uncertain. Compared with ordinary forecasting papers, it keeps the connected structure visible while forecasting.
ww: The approach works because it matches the shape of the real problem. In a dynamical network, uncertainty is not an afterthought added after prediction; it is one of the forces that determines the prediction. If unknown contact patterns are treated as fixed, an epidemic model may look precise while being wrong for the reason that matters most. If renewable supply is treated as a known number, a power reliability assessment can miss the cases where demand and generation move in an unlucky combination. By pushing uncertain inputs through the same network dynamics that produce the forecast, uncertainty quantification shows where confidence is justified and where it is fragile. It also helps separate harmless noise from dangerous uncertainty. Some link-weight variation may barely affect synchronization, while a small change in a key bridge link may change whether a cascade spreads. That distinction is exactly what a one-run model cannot reveal. The method is useful because it turns ignorance into an object that can be inspected, compared, and reduced.
po: The payoff is a clearer way to study adaptive social networks, neural plasticity, epidemiology, power systems, and similar connected systems when the available knowledge is incomplete or noisy. The abstract promises a tutorial that gives participants a comprehensive understanding of how dynamical networks and uncertainty quantification interact. The practical capability is better reliability of conclusions: instead of reporting only one predicted outbreak, stability result, synchronization pattern, or cascade risk, an analyst can report how uncertain structure, parameters, and outside influences affect that conclusion. That supports decisions about what to measure next, which assumptions matter, and where a prediction should be treated cautiously.
limits: The input describes a three-hour tutorial, not a paper presenting one new tested method, so the abstract does not prove accuracy gains, provide datasets, or compare algorithms. Its usefulness depends on whether the uncertain pieces can be described honestly from data or expert knowledge. If the possible contact patterns, edge weights, transmission rates, demand changes, or outside shocks are badly guessed, the quantified uncertainty may look careful while still being misleading. It also assumes the chosen dynamic model captures the main way influence moves through the network. If the model leaves out a critical mechanism, measuring uncertainty inside that model will not fix the missing mechanism.
